screening_decisions.reason: This study uses quantitative methods (secondary analysis of survey data, logistic regression) rather than qualitative methods. Additionally, it focuses on birth attendants and childbirth practices, not rehabilitation services.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews, phenomenological framework, and grounded theory. Explores experiences of stroke patients and family members about home-based exercise delivery after discharge from hospital, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation experiences.

Qualitative study using interpretative phenomenology, semi-structured interviews, and thematic analysis. Explores experiences and perceptions of SCI patients and healthcare professionals about a web-based self-management portal for physical activity, which constitutes telerehabilitation.

Mixed methods study with qualitative components (focus group interviews, case note analyses). Directly evaluates home-based occupational therapy for Parkinson's patients and caregivers, exploring experiences and factors affecting intervention delivery.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews. Explores patients' reasons for non-participation/non-adherence to home-based cardiac rehabilitation programs, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation experiences and barriers.
This is a systematic review of RCTs, not a qualitative study. Does not meet the methodological criteria.

While this is a qualitative evidence synthesis, it focuses on doctor-nurse substitution in primary care, not on home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services. The topic is outside the scope of the review.
This is a systematic review of experimental and observational studies, not a qualitative study. Does not meet the methodological criteria.

Qualitative study using grounded theory methodology and interviews. Explores behavioural patterns of adherence to home-based inspiratory muscle training in COPD patients, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation experiences.

Mixed methods study with qualitative component (semi-structured telephone interviews). Evaluates patients' perspectives and experiences on home tele-rehabilitation system for rheumatic patients, directly addressing telerehabilitation experiences.

Qualitative study using interpretive phenomenological design and semi-structured interviews. Explores experiences of rural/remote residents receiving rehabilitation intervention, including discussion of telehealth/telerehabilitation options.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews. Explores user needs and specifications for a home-based arm rehabilitation system for stroke patients, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation technology development.

Qualitative usability study with semi-structured interviews and content analysis. Explores experiences of people with aphasia and clinicians using an asynchronous telerehabilitation platform for home therapy, directly addressing telerehabilitation.

Qualitative study using thematic analysis, cultural probes, and interviews. Examines stroke survivors' experiences and requirements for home-based robotic rehabilitation technology, directly addressing telerehabilitation design.

While this is a qualitative evidence synthesis, it focuses on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health (RMNCAH) via mobile devices, not on rehabilitation services. The topic is outside the scope of the review.
This is a systematic review of RCTs, controlled trials, and other quantitative study designs, not a qualitative study. Does not meet the methodological criteria.

Mixed methods study with qualitative components. Evaluates feasibility and experiences of lung cancer survivors using a web-accessible home-based exercise program and ambulant monitoring, directly addressing telerehabilitation/home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using grounded theory with focus groups and interviews. Explores the transition process between hospital and continued home-based rehabilitation for stroke patients, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation experiences.

Qualitative content analysis using semi-structured interviews. Explores physical therapists' perspectives on patients' adherence to home exercise recommendations for spinal cord injury, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation.

Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews. Investigates experiences of informal caregivers in rehabilitation-in-the-home (RITH) programs, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation services and caregiver experiences.
This is a theoretical framework development paper describing the CFIR, not an empirical qualitative study exploring experiences with home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation.

Qualitative action research study using interviews. Directly explores organization and cooperation in home-based rehabilitation services in Norwegian boroughs, involving healthcare staff perspectives on home-based rehabilitation delivery.
This is a systematic rapid review, not a qualitative study. Does not meet the methodological criteria.

Qualitative study protocol using focus groups and interviews. Explores patient and healthcare provider experiences with eHealth/digital media for chronic illness management, including rehabilitation professionals. While broad, it includes rehabilitation professionals and addresses digital health for self-management which relates to telerehabilitation.

Qualitative study exploring patient perceptions of telephone-delivered exercise therapy (telerehabilitation) for knee OA. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, patient population, and telerehabilitation experiences.

Qualitative study exploring practices of support personnel in home-based reablement services. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, healthcare providers/staff, and home-based rehabilitation context.

Study develops a classification system (taxonomy) based on expert input, not exploring experiences/perceptions of patients, caregivers, or providers about service provision. Does not meet population or outcome criteria.

Primary design is a pilot case series with quantitative outcome measures and descriptive statistics. While satisfaction was reported, the methods are not primarily qualitative for data collection/analysis as required.
Systematic review of RCTs/CCTs. Not a primary qualitative study.
Mixed methods study with qualitative component (interviews) exploring experiences of veterans and caregivers with home telehealth. Matches criteria.
Qualitative study exploring patient experiences of a web-based home intervention. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, patients, and telerehabilitation/home-based context.
Qualitative study (phenomenological-hermeneutic) exploring patient experiences of cardiac tele-rehabilitation. Matches criteria.
Opinion/Report paper describing an event. Not a primary research study with qualitative data collection/analysis.
Qualitative study exploring patient experiences and acceptability of home-based exercise programs and gaming technology. Matches criteria.
Qualitative study exploring patient experiences of therapy and transition to home (home-based inpatient program). Matches criteria.

Qualitative phenomenological study exploring lived experiences of burn survivors in home care. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, patients, and home-based care/rehab.
Qualitative study exploring reasons/behaviors of caregivers providing informal rehabilitation at home. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, caregivers, and home-based rehab.
Qualitative study exploring clinician perceptions of wearable technology for home-based rehabilitation. Matches criteria for qualitative methods, healthcare providers, and home-based context.

Qualitative case study exploring factors enabling/constraining telerehabilitation routine use involving professionals, patients, and families. Matches criteria.
Mixed methods study with qualitative component (interviews) exploring patient experiences/acceptability of digital cardiac rehabilitation. Matches criteria.

This mixed methods study includes qualitative components (focus groups and semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis) exploring user experiences and perceptions about a web-based rehabilitation program, which aligns with telerehabilitation services.
This is a methodological guidance paper about assessing confidence in qualitative evidence syntheses, not a primary qualitative study about home-based rehabilitation services.

While this uses qualitative methods (focus groups), it focuses on physical activity information delivery preferences, not on experiences with home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services provision.
This is a literature review that classifies home-based rehabilitation programs. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis.

This qualitative study uses interviews with 35 patients and 12 staff members to explore experiences of being offered a choice between home-based and hospital-based cardiac rehabilitation, directly addressing home-based rehabilitation provision.
This is a Cochrane review protocol assessing effectiveness and cost of hospital at home services. It is not a primary qualitative study.

This qualitative study uses grounded theory approach with continuous interviews of three older adults receiving home-based rehabilitation, exploring their perceptions and experiences of staff collaboration during rehabilitation.

This mixed methods study includes qualitative components (thematic analysis of interviews) exploring user experiences with a mobile app for adapted exercise, which represents telerehabilitation services for people with physical disabilities.
This is a Cochrane review protocol assessing effects of home-based survivorship programmes. It is not a primary qualitative study.

The abstract describes a case presentation of neurocysticercosis, not a qualitative study about home rehabilitation after stroke. The title and abstract content do not match, and the study does not meet the selection criteria.

While this uses qualitative methods (thematic analysis of interviews), it focuses on phase III outpatient cardiac rehabilitation attendance barriers. It does not specifically address home-based rehabilitation or telerehabilitation services provision.
This appears to be a chapter or overview providing history and concepts of telerehabilitation, not a primary qualitative study with data collection and analysis.
This is a systematic review comparing outcomes of home-based versus inpatient rehabilitation. It does not use qualitative methods for data collection and analysis.

This mixed methods study includes qualitative data collection (semi-structured interviews, questionnaires) exploring patient experiences and perceptions of a telerehabilitation app for coronary artery disease patients.

This mixed methods study includes qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews with patients and practitioners about their experiences with a telerehabilitation model using videoconferencing for chronic back disorder management.

The abstract describes a cross-sectional study about TB notification among private practitioners in India, not about TBI rehabilitation or home-based rehabilitation services. Title and abstract do not match.

This mixed methods study includes qualitative components (semi-structured interviews at baseline and 3 months) exploring barriers and facilitators to home-based cycling rehabilitation in older patients with lumbar spinal stenosis.

This qualitative focus group study explores factors influencing eRehabilitation uptake among stroke patients, informal caregivers, and healthcare professionals, directly addressing telerehabilitation service provision.

This is a cross-sectional study measuring sitting workspace using a device. It does not use qualitative methods and the abstract content does not match the title about telemedicine during natural disasters.

This is a meeting document about rehabilitation definition methodology, not a primary qualitative study about home-based rehabilitation services.

While qualitative methods are used, this study focuses on technology development and validation of a BCI system rather than exploring experiences, perceptions, or behaviours about home-based rehabilitation provision. The primary aim is developing/validating a technological intervention.

The abstract does not match the title - it describes a quantitative study about health care utilization estimates in older German adults, not a qualitative study about assistive technologies or home-based rehabilitation. Does not meet selection criteria.
